title: Caché - San Francisco
text: Design and development of French bistro in San Francisco.
label: Discover

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

November 2024 - January 2025

Role:

Product Design (UX/UI) - Web Developer

Tools:

Figma, WordPress, HTML, CSS
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

Caché is a modern neighborhood bistro in San Francisco that blends a relaxed French bistro atmosphere with contemporary culinary experiences. The restaurant needed a digital presence that reflected its identity, provided essential information, and facilitated reservations while optimizing for both desktop and mobile users.

The challenge was to create a website that not only showcased the brand's unique personality but also delivered a seamless user experience for customers seeking details about the menu, reservations, and events.

Understanding the Audience

Before opening Figma, I sat down with the owners to walk through a typical week at the restaurant: who books ahead, who walks in, who comes back. That conversation, combined with a look at comparable San Francisco bistro sites, shaped three audience groups I designed around:

  1. Local Residents & Tourists : Seeking an elevated but welcoming dining experience, usually deciding same-day or same-week.
  2. Food Enthusiasts & Millennials : Interested in modern gastronomy and natural wines, more likely to check the menu and Instagram before booking.
  3. Casual & Special Occasion Diners : Exploring options for brunch, happy hour, or dinner, often comparing a handful of restaurants before committing.

The common thread across all three was that people wanted to see the menu and make a reservation within a couple of taps, without digging through a cluttered homepage. That became the north star for the layout: menu and booking always one click away, never buried under marketing copy.

details.title: Design Approach & Strategy
lines: The design focused on elegance and warmth, capturing the bistro's inviting yet sophisticated atmosphere. Key elements included:

1. Color Palette

    2. I selected a terra cotta shade (#B86C51) that evokes warmth and a natural feel, complemented by an off-white background (#FBEBD9) to create a clean and airy aesthetic.

1. Custom Logo Design

    2. Instead of using an existing font, I hand-wrote the restaurant's name on paper, scanned it, and vectorized it to create a unique and personal brand identity. This gave the logo a handcrafted, distinctive feel.

1. Typography
    2. The main text fonts are Ruffina for its refined and expressive character, paired with Lato for a modern and highly readable contrast.
  2. Icons & Visual Accents
    3. I designed additional custom icons, including an Instagram logo, a fish, and a carrot, allowing flexibility for the client to add visual markers for social media, seafood, or vegetarian dishes.

details.txt:
Development & Implementation

Using WordPress as the CMS allowed for flexible content management while ensuring smooth performance. Custom HTML and CSS were incorporated to refine styling beyond standard templates, ensuring brand consistency. Specific optimizations included:
  • A fully responsive menu and booking system
  • Fast-loading pages with optimized media content
  • SEO best practices to enhance discoverability

away.title: Take-aways
text: The site launched with the menu and reservation flow front and center, which is exactly what the owners had asked for after seeing how many of their regulars were booking from their phones.
Building the logo from a scanned, hand-written mark instead of a stock font turned out to be the detail people mentioned most. It gave the brand a handmade feel that matched the food.
Working inside WordPress also meant the owners could update the menu themselves once I handed the site off, which mattered more to them long-term than any single design decision I made.

If I revisited this project, I'd push for a short round of user testing with real diners before launch rather than relying on my own walkthroughs, since a couple of the reservation-flow tweaks I made post-launch would have surfaced earlier.

title: The Collectible
text: Co-founded an auction-house marketplace for authenticated collectibles. Product design and UX for B2C + B2B, prototyped in Figma.
label: Read More

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

January 2023 - August 2024

Role:

Co-Founder, CTO & Product Designer

Tools:

Figma, Flutter, Dart, Firebase, GCP
details.txt:
Context

TheCollectible is a marketplace I co-founded to make authenticated collectibles accessible: pieces that come from auction houses, sold at a fair price to collectors and amateurs. The product problem was trust and access: people who wanted a specific work could not easily find provenance, estimates, or a clean buying path outside the auction room.

I designed the full product in Figma: a public B2C site (homepage, artwork detail, artists, favorites, auth) and a B2B dashboard for auction houses (catalogue, estimates, tracking, invoices). Those frames are the source of the screens in this case study.

Brand & landing

The brand needed to feel like a house of auction, not a generic shop. Deep green, cream, and a serif wordmark. The marketing landing explains the offer in one sentence (authenticated objects from auction houses, at accessible prices), then walks through how it works, what an auction is, and who is behind the product.

Two entry points sit on the hero: Explorer les ventes for browsers, Se connecter for returning collectors. The illustrated landing (line drawings, newsletter, team) was designed to feel human and light next to the more formal marketplace.

Marketing site

The illustrated landing page (Figma: Landing Page / Final) is the story layer: newsletter capture, a three-step “comment ça marche”, an explainer on auctions, and a team block. I treated this as a separate surface from the marketplace so the product UI could stay quiet and the brand page could carry the personality.
details.alt: TheCollectible illustrated landing page from Figma

details.txt:
Artwork detail, where trust lives

The listing page is the core of the B2C product. Price, estimate range, dimensions, medium, artist, and a short description sit next to a large object photo, with a thumbnail strip and related works in the same category.

That layout came from research: collectors would not buy from a thumbnail and a price. Provenance and estimates had to be visible before “Acheter maintenant” or “Favoris”. Search by name or artist stays in the header so someone arriving with a specific piece in mind never has to start over.
details.alt: TheCollectible artwork detail page from Figma

details.txt:
B2B dashboard

Auction houses needed a different product: lots listed vs sold, yearly results, conversion, and recent orders. The dashboard (Tableau de bord) is the first screen after login, with a sidebar for Catalogue, Estimations, Suivi, Réglages, Factures, and Compte.

I designed it as a working tool, not a marketing page: charts first, house switcher in the header, export later in the catalogue. The house (e.g. Drouot) is the account context for every number on the page.

Catalogue, the operational table

The catalogue is how a house manages lots: title, description, photo, price, provenance, post date, status (en cours, actif, vendu). Bulk actions, search, export, and “soumettre lot(s)” sit at the top so a busy operator can work from one table.

This is the other half of the trust problem. If the house cannot keep provenance and status accurate, the public listing page fails. I designed both screens as one system.

Design system

The palette is short on purpose: cream, sage, forest green, near-black. Green is the brand and the primary action; cream is the page; sage is the illustrated landing. I kept the marketplace chrome white so object photos stay the focus, and used the dark green for hero, footer, and primary buttons.

The same logo, header, and button language run across B2C and B2B so a house employee and a collector still feel they are in the same product.

details.title: What I designed in Figma
details.subtitle: The prototype covers two products sharing one system:
lines: • B2C marketplace
Homepage (hero, categories, about), artwork detail, artist list and artist detail, favorites, orders, sign up and log in.
• B2B house tools
Dashboard, catalogue, estimates, tracking, settings, invoices, account.
• Brand & system
Logo, type, color palette, illustrations, and the illustrated marketing landing.
• Build
Flutter/Dart on Firebase/GCP for the shared app. Figma stayed the source of truth for UX before and during development.

away.title: Takeaways
text: The product only works if both sides of the table are designed together. A beautiful artwork page is useless if the house cannot keep provenance and lot status accurate in the catalogue. Designing B2C and B2B in the same Figma file forced those two screens to share one system.

Trust is not a visual style. On this project it meant estimate ranges next to price, a search that starts from artist or object name, and a dashboard a house can actually operate. I said no to extra marketplace features until those three things were solid.

title: Divorce.fm
text: Development of an online radio with a self-managed CMS.
label: Read More

details.box:
Overview

Timeline:

January 2024 - August 2024

Role:

Web Developer

Tools:

PHP, Laravel, MySQL, Tailwind CSS, Alpine.js, SoundCloud API
details.txt:
Background & Challenge

The client wanted an online radio built around SoundCloud mixes, with a deliberately old-school, slightly chaotic feel: random backgrounds, a hue-shifting logo, playful button art. The visual direction and branding came from the friend I built the site with. My job was turning that into a real site the client could run day to day.

The brief also included self-management: the client needed to add new mixes and swap background images without calling me every time. That made the real engineering problem the admin panel, not the player.

details.title: The Radio Player
lines: The public-facing side is plain JavaScript wrapped around the SoundCloud widget: play, pause, skip, and a volume control that occasionally lands on a joke value instead of a real percentage, because the client wanted the whole thing to feel a bit unserious. The logo and buttons get a random hue shift on load, and long track titles scroll like a vintage marquee instead of being cut off.

Ads are skipped on mobile on purpose: autoplaying a sponsor track over mobile data felt like the wrong default. The palette stayed deliberately minimal (black and white with a single accent color) so the background images the client uploads stay the focal point.

details.title: Two Versions, One Site
lines: The first version shipped in July 2024: a plain PHP and MySQL site running on Apache, built fast to get the client something real to test and use. Once it was clear the admin side needed to do more than a login form and a few uploads, I rebuilt the backend in Laravel over the following months, with Breeze handling authentication and a proper admin panel replacing the hand-rolled one.

details.txt:
The Admin Panel

Once rebuilt in Laravel, the admin panel became the core of the product. The client pastes a raw SoundCloud link and the app parses artist and title straight out of the URL, with no manual data entry. A separate pool of sponsor tracks plays between mixes, chosen by whichever has been played least, so no single ad gets overplayed.

Background images can be uploaded one at a time or dropped as a folder. The app syncs them into the database and resizes and compresses each one automatically, including animated GIFs. If the database connection drops, the site falls back to a maintenance page instead of crashing. A radio going down felt worse than most sites going down.

details.title: What the Admin Panel Actually Does
details.subtitle: Once rebuilt in Laravel, the panel handled:
lines: • Track management
The admin pastes a raw SoundCloud link and the app parses the artist and title straight out of the URL, no manual data entry.
• Ad rotation
A separate pool of sponsor tracks plays between mixes, chosen by whichever has been played the least, so no single ad gets overplayed.
• Background management
The client uploads images directly, or drops a folder of files and the app syncs them into the database. Every image gets resized and compressed automatically, including animated GIFs.
• Fallback handling
If the database connection drops, the site falls back to a maintenance page instead of crashing. A radio station going down felt worse than most sites going down.

details.txt:
Color & Visual Identity

The palette stayed deliberately minimal (black and white with a single accent color) so the background images the client uploads stay the focal point instead of competing with the UI. The accent color shifts hue on every page load, giving each visit a slightly different feel without changing the structure.

details.title: Launch commercial

away.title: Takeaways
text: This project taught me when to rebuild instead of patch. The first PHP version got the client live fast, but once the admin requirements grew past a login form and a few uploads, hand-rolling that in plain PHP would have meant reinventing a framework badly. Moving to Laravel for the second version gave the client a panel that actually holds up: real authentication, validated uploads, and image processing that doesn't need me on call every time they want to add a background.
It's also the project where I got comfortable telling a client that a feature belongs behind a real framework instead of stacking more custom PHP on top of what was already there.
